title: Hyrcanus and his brother Aristobulus
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman writes: The sons of King Yannai, whose mother was the great woman known as Queen Shelamzion, sister of Shimon ben Shetach, whose reign was the happiest period for Israel in all the days of the Second Temple. When she died, her two sons began to quarrel over the kingship, and they themselves handed the people of Israel over to the mighty Pompey, general of the Roman army, and brought destruction upon the people. This is mentioned in Sotah 49b: Our Rabbis taught: When the Hasmonean kings besieged one another, Hyrcanus was outside and Aristobulus inside. Each day they would lower denarii in a basket and haul up the daily offerings for them. There was an old man there who was versed in Greek wisdom. He said to them (the besiegers): As long as they carry out the Temple service, they will not be delivered into your hands. The next day — they hauled up a pig for them. When it reached halfway up the wall, it dug its claws into the wall and the Land of Israel shook four hundred parasangs. Hyman interprets this as meaning that then the entire Land of Israel was delivered into the hands of the swine. And Rashi, in his holy language, says at the end of chapter 6 of Song of Songs, on the verse "I knew not my soul; it set me among the chariots of my princely people" (Song of Songs 6:12), that the dispute that grew strong among the Hasmonean kings Hyrcanus and Aristobulus was such that one of them brought Roman rule upon them and became its servant; Hyman adds that his end was that Herod killed him when he was an old man of more than eighty years.

notes.text: Hyman’s praise of the queen’s reign and his interpretation of the swine episode as Roman subjugation remain his prose. The referent of the final Herod/over-eighty pronoun remains unresolved; no modern historical harmonization is imposed.

The praise of Queen Shelamzion's reign, the brothers' responsibility for Roman intervention, and the interpretation of the swine episode as Roman subjugation are explicitly presented as Hyman's assertions. This preserves his affirmative force without independently verifying the historical synthesis. The source's הגבור is rendered mighty; its general-of-the-Roman-army description remains. The supplied Sotah49b and end-of-chapter6 Song of Songs/Rashi locators are retained, without a fresh whole named primary passage or printed-page collation. The final one-of-them, its servant, his end, Herod, and over-eighty referents remain as Hyman gives them; no brother is selected and no modern chronological repair is imposed. All earlier English and notes, including the original printed-wording claim, remain archived rather than newly verified. The original mixed current note is preserved verbatim. The source hold remains.

The whole consulted Sotah 49b paragraphs have Hyrcanus outside and Aristobulus inside, the daily offerings, Greek wisdom, the pig and four hundred parasangs. Hyman’s interpretation of the swine as Roman subjugation is his historical reading; the longer Gemara’s subsequent decrees are not inserted into his abridgment. The whole consulted Rashi on Song of Songs 6:12 has one of the brothers bringing Roman rule, receiving kingship from its hand and becoming its servant. Its three comments do not include the final clause about Herod and an age of over eighty found in Hyman’s notice; that clause is retained as Hyman’s report, with the pronoun unassigned. The exact older printing behind his account has not been collated. His praise of Queen Shelamzion, the family identifications, Pompey’s role and historical evaluation remain attributed to him, without selecting a brother or imposing a modern chronology.
